scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire paper (Azhir et al. 2025, Med) develops and validates a computational 'precision phenotyping' algorithm for identifying post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC/long COVID) from EHR data; it contains no discussion of Lyme disease anywhere in the text.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a peer-reviewed methods study that built and validated a computational algorithm to identify patients with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC, i.e., long COVID) from electronic health record data across 14 hospitals and 20 community health centers in Massachusetts (Mass General Brigham system). Using records from over 295,000 patients, the algorithm flagged 24,360 'long-haulers' among 85,364 COVID-19 cases (an adjusted prevalence of 22.8%) with 79.9% precision, which the authors say outperforms the standard U09.9 ICD-10 diagnosis code (77.8% precision in their own chart review) and shows less demographic bias in who gets identified as having long COVID. The paper documents that relying on diagnosis codes alone (U09.9) captures far fewer and a demographically skewed subset of likely PASC patients, and it reports which organ systems are most affected and how the odds of PASC differ by sex, race/ethnicity, and age. It contains no dollar costs, no direct/indirect economic burden figures, no insurance/access-barrier data, and no Lyme disease content of any kind.

contextual_issues: Multi-organ PASC burden (patients experiencing systemic, cardiovascular, GI, neurological, mental-health, and other organ-specific sequelae simultaneously, with 13% having more than one PASC and 4% more than three) is reported in clinical terms but not translated into any economic, caregiving-time, or productivity measure.

The paper describes race/age differences in the odds of developing organ-specific PASC (e.g., Black patients had significantly higher odds in skin, renal/GU, neurologic, cardiovascular, and systemic categories; Asian and Hispanic patients had lower odds in specific systems; gynecological, skin, and psychiatric PASC had higher odds in patients under 45; eye/ear, endocrine, musculoskeletal, and renal/GU PASC were more common in older patients), but the underlying odds ratios with confidence intervals are reported only in a supplemental table (Table S4) not included in the extracted text.

The difficulty of reliably identifying PASC patients (described as lacking a 'scalable, universally accepted algorithm') implies downstream patient-level effects such as delayed recognition or inconsistent care pathways, but the document does not quantify diagnostic delay, repeated care-seeking, or insurance/access barriers.
No mention of out-of-pocket costs, direct non-medical costs (travel, paid help), lost income, or caregiving burden anywhere in the document.
evidence_gaps: No direct medical cost, indirect cost (lost income, productivity), direct non-medical cost, or caregiving-time data are reported for long COVID in this document.
No Lyme disease data of any kind (reported cases, cost, burden) appear in this document.
No data on insurance coverage, access barriers, or time-to-diagnosis duration are reported.

Organ-specific case counts and prevalence/precision estimates come from one integrated health system in one state over one defined study period and cannot be assumed nationally representative without further data.

Full odds-ratio estimates with confidence intervals (Table S4) and the complete CCSR category list (Tables S2-S3) are referenced but not available in the extracted text, limiting the granularity of demographic/organ-level burden that could be modeled.
No price-year-anchored dollar figures exist in this document to ground any economic simulator component for either condition.
comparison_boundaries: Do not pool the algorithm's own EHR-cohort prevalence estimates (raw 28.5%; PPV-adjusted 22.8%; population: 85,364 COVID-19 cases in the MGB system, infections 03/2020-06/2023, 12-month follow-up) with the NCHS Household Pulse Survey estimate (24.0%; population: Massachusetts adults, survey period June 1, 2022-October 2, 2023) as a single low/high range - these differ in case-ascertainment method (EHR/algorithmic phenotyping of lab/diagnosis-confirmed infections vs. self-reported general-adult survey), population definition, and measurement time window, even though the paper itself juxtaposes them for rough comparison.

Do not treat the U09.9 ICD-10-code-based counts (6,340 coded patients, only 62.6% with confirmed COVID-19, adjusted to 'under 5,000' via 77.8% PPV) and the precision-algorithm-identified cohort (24,360 long-haulers, 79.9% PPV) as alternate-confidence estimates of one quantity - they use structurally different case-finding methods (single diagnosis code vs. multi-step attention-based exclusion algorithm applied to the full cohort) and are not simply a low/high range of the same measurement.

Organ-specific case counts and prevalence percentages apply only to the MGB Massachusetts cohort over the stated study period and should not be extrapolated to national or other-state populations without explicit reweighting.
This document contains no Lyme disease content; none of its figures should be combined or compared with Lyme disease data from any other source.

sex_gender_findings.finding: The paper reports that, after correcting for demographics and comorbidities, women had significantly higher odds of developing systemic, GI, neurological, skin, mental-health-related, musculoskeletal, and gynecological PASC than men; odds of respiratory, renal/genitourinary, endocrine, and eyes-and-ears PASC did not reach statistical significance between sexes (p value <0.05 threshold, per the document's own reporting). It also reports sex composition differences in diagnosed/identified cohorts: 67.5% female among U09.9-coded patients and 64.5% female among algorithm-identified long-haulers, versus 62.6% female among the overall COVID-19 case cohort and 51% female in the Massachusetts census population.

claims_undercounting_caveat.basis: Both the algorithm-derived PASC cohort and the U09.9 comparator are built from structured ICD-10-CM/CCSR diagnosis and procedure codes extracted from the Mass General Brigham EHR research repository (STAR Methods describes use of 'ICD-10 diagnosis and procedure codes'). The paper itself states in its Limitations that 'Our reliance on structured data may have resulted in an underestimation of PASC,' and separately documents that the U09.9 diagnosis code is both imprecise (PPV 77.8% in this cohort's chart review, 40-65% in cited prior work) and demographically skewed (toward White, female patients relative to the Massachusetts census) - consistent with a claims/ICD-10/EHR-coded undercounting mechanism.

scientific_analysis.disease_focus_rationale: The entire paper (Azhir et al. 2025, Med) develops and validates a computational 'precision phenotyping' algorithm for identifying post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC/long COVID) from EHR data; it contains no discussion of Lyme disease anywhere in the text.
scientific_analysis.plain_language_summary: This is a peer-reviewed methods study that built and validated a computational algorithm to identify patients with post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC, i.e., long COVID) from electronic health record data across 14 hospitals and 20 community health centers in Massachusetts (Mass General Brigham system). Using records from over 295,000 patients, the algorithm flagged 24,360 'long-haulers' among 85,364 COVID-19 cases (an adjusted prevalence of 22.8%) with 79.9% precision, which the authors say outperforms the standard U09.9 ICD-10 diagnosis code (77.8% precision in their own chart review) and shows less demographic bias in who gets identified as having long COVID. The paper documents that relying on diagnosis codes alone (U09.9) captures far fewer and a demographically skewed subset of likely PASC patients, and it reports which organ systems are most affected and how the odds of PASC differ by sex, race/ethnicity, and age. It contains no dollar costs, no direct/indirect economic burden figures, no insurance/access-barrier data, and no Lyme disease content of any kind.

spec.title: Long COVID (PASC) Case-Finding Precision and Demographic Skew Simulator
spec.boundary: This simulator covers only what Azhir et al. (2025, Med) measured: how precisely a computational phenotyping algorithm versus the standard U09.9 diagnosis code identifies likely long COVID ('PASC', post-acute sequelae of COVID-19) patients from electronic health records at one Massachusetts health system (Mass General Brigham), including how demographically representative each method's identified group is. It contains no dollar costs, productivity loss, caregiving burden, insurance/access data, or Lyme disease content of any kind. All counts and percentages apply only to this one health system's 2020-2023 COVID-19 case cohort and should not be treated as nationally representative.

takeaway.patient: This study, from one Massachusetts hospital system rather than a national sample, found that relying on the official long-COVID diagnosis code alone identified far fewer patients as having lingering post-COVID symptoms than a newer computational method did, and that the people who ended up with that diagnosis code were disproportionately White and female compared with the state's overall population. The researchers' own corrected estimate suggests a meaningfully larger share of people with COVID-19 may have had lingering symptoms than the diagnosis code alone would suggest. This describes patterns in one health system's records, not any individual's own diagnosis or risk.
takeaway.care: Within this one Massachusetts health system, the official U09.9 diagnosis code captured a smaller and more demographically skewed (whiter, more female) set of likely PASC patients than a precision-phenotyping algorithm applied to the same records, even though the code itself was reasonably precise (about 78% of chart-reviewed U09.9 cases were confirmed). The algorithm's own precision-adjusted estimate suggests roughly a fifth to a quarter of COVID-19 cases in this cohort may have had a persistent post-acute symptom cluster - a notably larger and less demographically skewed group than code-based counts alone would surface.
takeaway.policy: In this single Massachusetts health system's EHR cohort, diagnosis-code-based case counts substantially understated the algorithm-estimated long-hauler population, and the code-identified group skewed toward White, female patients relative to the Massachusetts census, while the algorithm-identified group showed somewhat less skew. The paper's own precision-adjusted estimate (about 22.8% of COVID-19 cases) is a corrected estimate from this cohort, not a validated national prevalence figure, and the two case-finding methods are structurally different rather than simple low/high bounds on one true number.

patient: If you have ongoing symptoms after COVID-19 but have not received a formal long-COVID diagnosis code, this research suggests the absence of a code does not necessarily mean a lingering condition isn't real - it may be worth raising persistent symptoms with a clinician again.

When comparing your own experience to long-COVID statistics you encounter elsewhere, keep in mind these particular percentages come from one Massachusetts hospital system over a specific multi-year period, not a national count.

If you are involved with a patient advocacy group, this finding about who does and doesn't end up with a long-COVID diagnosis code (skewed toward White, female patients in this cohort) could be useful context for asking whether identification efforts in your own area adequately reach men and patients of other races and ethnicities.
care: Consider comparing your own system's U09.9 diagnosis-code precision against this cohort's own chart-reviewed figure (about 78% precision) before treating code-based counts alone as a complete picture of your long-COVID patient population.

This finding on demographic skew in diagnosis-code-identified cohorts (over-representation of White, female patients relative to the Massachusetts census, with somewhat less skew in the algorithm-identified group) may be worth checking against your own clinic's referral and diagnosis patterns.

Because this is a single-health-system, Massachusetts-based study over one defined period, treat its prevalence and precision figures as hypothesis-generating for your own population rather than a direct capacity-planning number, pending local validation.

If evaluating or building a similar EHR-based phenotyping approach, note the authors' own stated limitation that reliance on structured diagnosis/procedure codes may still underestimate true PASC cases.
policy: Use this study's own evidence that diagnosis-code-based counts (an estimated well under 5,000 confirmed cases among 6,340 coded patients) substantially understate the algorithm-estimated long-hauler population in the same cohort, while noting these are two structurally different case-finding methods, not simply low and high bounds on one true number.

Consider whether surveillance or program metrics that rely on a single ICD-10 diagnosis code adequately capture men and non-White patients, given this study's documented demographic skew in code-based identification relative to the Massachusetts census.

Treat this single-health-system, Massachusetts-specific estimate as one input to need estimation rather than a national prevalence figure, and seek corroborating data before using it for funding or eligibility decisions.

## Source and Scope
This simulator is built from Azhir et al. (2025, *Med*), a methods study validating a computational algorithm for identifying post-acute sequelae of COVID-19 (PASC, i.e., long COVID) from electronic health records at Mass General Brigham, Massachusetts, across 85,364 adult COVID-19 cases (infections 03/2020-06/2023, 12-month follow-up). It is not a cost-of-illness study: it contains no dollar figures, productivity-loss estimates, or caregiving-burden data, and no Lyme disease content.

## Parameters
Inputs include the raw algorithm-flagged PASC share (28.5%), the algorithm's chart-review-confirmed precision (79.9%), the standard U09.9 diagnosis code's precision (77.8%, with the paper citing 40-65% in prior literature), the raw U09.9-coded patient count (6,340), the total COVID-19 case cohort size (85,364), and the female share among U09.9-coded versus algorithm-identified patients (67.5% vs. 64.5%, against a cited Massachusetts census female share of 51%). All slider ranges beyond each stated default are assumed exploration bounds chosen for this simulator, not values specified in the source.

## Limitations
**Undercounting**: The paper relies on structured ICD-10-CM/CCSR diagnosis and procedure codes extracted from the EHR, and states in its own Limitations that this reliance 'may have resulted in an underestimation of PASC.' The U09.9 code itself is imprecise (77.8% precision in this cohort's chart review, 40-65% in cited prior work) and demographically skewed toward White, female patients relative to the Massachusetts census - so diagnosis-code-based counts likely undercount and skew the true patient population.

**No subgroup breakdown of pooled figures**: The headline prevalence (22.8%/28.5%) and precision figures (79.9%/77.8%) are reported as single Massachusetts-wide pooled values, not broken out by sex, age, or race/ethnicity, even though the same paper separately reports organ-specific odds ratios by these same characteristics elsewhere. Federal survey data such as NHIS and BRFSS generally supports disaggregated analysis even though this document did not perform it here.

**System-level gap**: The paper describes a broader infrastructure problem: as of publication there was no scalable, universally accepted algorithm or diagnosis code for identifying PASC patients, which the authors say has hindered enrollment in large-scale clinical studies of potential therapies.

All figures describe one integrated health system over one study period and should not be treated as nationally representative without further data.

## Federal cross-check (computed by the system, not by the AI model)

The model only read these quantities from the document; the comparisons below were calculated in code from federal data files. The federal figures are published or surveyed values; the simulator's own outputs are modeled from the uploaded document.

spec.title: Long COVID (PASC) Case-Finding Precision and Demographic Skew Simulator
spec.boundary: This simulator covers only what Azhir et al. (2025, Med) measured: how precisely a computational phenotyping algorithm versus the standard U09.9 diagnosis code identifies likely long COVID ('PASC', post-acute sequelae of COVID-19) patients from electronic health records at one Massachusetts health system (Mass General Brigham), including how demographically representative each method's identified group is. It contains no dollar costs, productivity loss, caregiving burden, insurance/access data, or Lyme disease content of any kind. All counts and percentages apply only to this one health system's 2020-2023 COVID-19 case cohort and should not be treated as nationally representative.

takeaway.patient: This study, from one Massachusetts hospital system rather than a national sample, found that relying on the official long-COVID diagnosis code alone identified far fewer patients as having lingering post-COVID symptoms than a newer computational method did, and that the people who ended up with that diagnosis code were disproportionately White and female compared with the state's overall population. The researchers' own corrected estimate suggests a meaningfully larger share of people with COVID-19 may have had lingering symptoms than the diagnosis code alone would suggest. This describes patterns in one health system's records, not any individual's own diagnosis or risk.
takeaway.care: Within this one Massachusetts health system, the official U09.9 diagnosis code captured a smaller and more demographically skewed (whiter, more female) set of likely PASC patients than a precision-phenotyping algorithm applied to the same records, even though the code itself was reasonably precise (about 78% of chart-reviewed U09.9 cases were confirmed). The algorithm's own precision-adjusted estimate suggests roughly a fifth to a quarter of COVID-19 cases in this cohort may have had a persistent post-acute symptom cluster - a notably larger and less demographically skewed group than code-based counts alone would surface.
takeaway.policy: In this single Massachusetts health system's EHR cohort, diagnosis-code-based case counts substantially understated the algorithm-estimated long-hauler population, and the code-identified group skewed toward White, female patients relative to the Massachusetts census, while the algorithm-identified group showed somewhat less skew. The paper's own precision-adjusted estimate (about 22.8% of COVID-19 cases) is a corrected estimate from this cohort, not a validated national prevalence figure, and the two case-finding methods are structurally different rather than simple low/high bounds on one true number.

patient: If you have ongoing symptoms after COVID-19 but have not received a formal long-COVID diagnosis code, this research suggests the absence of a code does not necessarily mean a lingering condition isn't real - it may be worth raising persistent symptoms with a clinician again.

When comparing your own experience to long-COVID statistics you encounter elsewhere, keep in mind these particular percentages come from one Massachusetts hospital system over a specific multi-year period, not a national count.

If you are involved with a patient advocacy group, this finding about who does and doesn't end up with a long-COVID diagnosis code (skewed toward White, female patients in this cohort) could be useful context for asking whether identification efforts in your own area adequately reach men and patients of other races and ethnicities.
care: Consider comparing your own system's U09.9 diagnosis-code precision against this cohort's own chart-reviewed figure (about 78% precision) before treating code-based counts alone as a complete picture of your long-COVID patient population.

This finding on demographic skew in diagnosis-code-identified cohorts (over-representation of White, female patients relative to the Massachusetts census, with somewhat less skew in the algorithm-identified group) may be worth checking against your own clinic's referral and diagnosis patterns.

Because this is a single-health-system, Massachusetts-based study over one defined period, treat its prevalence and precision figures as hypothesis-generating for your own population rather than a direct capacity-planning number, pending local validation.

If evaluating or building a similar EHR-based phenotyping approach, note the authors' own stated limitation that reliance on structured diagnosis/procedure codes may still underestimate true PASC cases.
policy: Use this study's own evidence that diagnosis-code-based counts (an estimated well under 5,000 confirmed cases among 6,340 coded patients) substantially understate the algorithm-estimated long-hauler population in the same cohort, while noting these are two structurally different case-finding methods, not simply low and high bounds on one true number.

Consider whether surveillance or program metrics that rely on a single ICD-10 diagnosis code adequately capture men and non-White patients, given this study's documented demographic skew in code-based identification relative to the Massachusetts census.

Treat this single-health-system, Massachusetts-specific estimate as one input to need estimation rather than a national prevalence figure, and seek corroborating data before using it for funding or eligibility decisions.

inputs.label: COVID-19 case cohort size
inputs.source: Results, cohort description (p.3); this is the stated total adult COVID-19 case count in the MGB EHR cohort; 50000-120000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the total number of COVID-19 cases in the Massachusetts health-system cohort the study analyzed; moving it changes how many patients the prevalence percentages below translate into as a count.

inputs.label: Raw algorithm-flagged PASC share

inputs.interpretation: This is the share of COVID-19 cases the algorithm flagged as having at least one post-acute symptom cluster, before correcting for the algorithm's own false-positive rate; adjusting it tests how sensitive the corrected prevalence estimate below is to the raw flagging rate.

inputs.label: Algorithm positive predictive value
inputs.source: Results, chart-review paragraph (p.3); 60-95 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of algorithm-flagged patients confirmed by chart review to actually have post-acute COVID-19 symptoms (positive predictive value, i.e., precision); lowering it shows how much of the raw flagged share would be false positives.

inputs.label: U09.9 diagnosis code positive predictive value
inputs.source: Results, chart-review paragraph (p.3), which also cites a 40-65% precision range from prior literature; 40-95 range is an assumed exploration bound covering both this cohort's own figure and the cited prior-literature range.
inputs.interpretation: This is how often a U09.9 long-COVID diagnosis code, chart-reviewed in this cohort, actually corresponded to a confirmed case; lowering it toward the 40-65% range the paper cites from prior studies shows how precision assumptions change the estimated true-case count below.

inputs.label: Patients with a U09.9 diagnosis code
inputs.source: Results (p.3); 2000-15000 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the raw count of patients who received the official long-COVID diagnosis code in this health system's records; it is the starting point for estimating how many of those code-based diagnoses are likely accurate.

inputs.label: Female share among U09.9-coded patients
inputs.source: Results (p.3) and Discussion bias paragraph (p.8); 50-80 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of women among patients who received the official diagnosis code, compared against the Massachusetts census female share of 51% the document cites; a higher value indicates the code-based cohort over-represents women relative to the general population.

inputs.label: Female share among algorithm-identified long-haulers
inputs.source: Results (p.3) and Discussion bias paragraph (p.8); 50-80 range is an assumed exploration bound, not from the source.
inputs.interpretation: This is the share of women among patients the precision algorithm identified as long-haulers; comparing it with the U09.9-coded share tests whether the algorithm's demographic skew is smaller than the diagnosis code's, as the document reports.

outputs.label: PPV-adjusted PASC prevalence
outputs.interpretation: This reproduces the document's own adjustment of the raw algorithm-flagged share for the algorithm's precision, matching its reported 22.8% adjusted prevalence estimate among COVID-19 cases in this one Massachusetts health system. The document does not call this the 'true' population prevalence, only its own corrected estimate, and it is structurally different from the separately-cited Household Pulse Survey figure, which used self-reported data from a general adult sample.

outputs.label: Estimated confirmed-PASC count among U09.9-coded patients
outputs.interpretation: This reproduces the document's own calculation (raw U09.9-coded count multiplied by that code's precision), which it describes as yielding 'under 5,000' true PASC patients among 6,340 coded patients. A lower value here means more of the official diagnosis-code count is likely a false positive rather than a confirmed long-COVID case.

outputs.label: Estimated PPV-adjusted long-hauler count (algorithm)
outputs.interpretation: This converts the document's own adjusted prevalence percentage into a patient count for the full COVID-19 case cohort. Comparing it with the estimated confirmed-PASC count among U09.9-coded patients illustrates the gap the paper highlights between algorithm-based and diagnosis-code-based case-finding, though the two methods are not simply low and high estimates of one true number - they use structurally different ascertainment approaches.

outputs.label: Female-share difference, algorithm cohort minus U09.9-coded cohort (percentage points; positive = algorithm cohort has a higher female share, negative = lower)
outputs.interpretation: A negative value (as reported: 64.5 minus 67.5 equals -3 percentage points) means the algorithm-identified cohort's female share sits closer to the Massachusetts census female share of 51% than the U09.9-coded cohort does, consistent with the document's finding that the algorithm shows somewhat less demographic skew than the diagnosis code alone. This does not mean the algorithm cohort is unbiased, only less skewed on this one measure.
